facts.text: NIOSH tested a radar-based proximity warning system on a Caterpillar 793B haul truck, with a payload class above 200 t, for seven days of normal operation covering loading, hauling, dumping, parking and maintenance manoeuvres.
facts.quote: NIOSH tested a radar-based proximity warning system on a Caterpillar 793B haul truck (payload class above 200 t) for seven days of normal operation, including loading, hauling, dumping, parking and maintenance manoeuvres [3, 2].

facts.text: Ruff defined a false proximity alarm as an alarm when the radar sensed no significant object in its zone; typical causes included small ruts, rocks, foliage and dirt features.
facts.quote: A **false** alarm occurred when the radar sensed no significant object in its zone; small ruts, rocks, foliage and dirt features were typical causes.

facts.text: Ruff defined a nuisance proximity alarm as a technically correct detection of an existing object with no urgent danger because the operator knew about the object and the task required approaching it.
facts.quote: A **nuisance** alarm was technically correct, the object existed, but there was no urgent danger because the operator knew about it and the task required the approach

facts.text: Backing toward a rock pile at a loading area was an example of a task-required approach that could produce a nuisance proximity alarm.
facts.quote: for example backing toward a rock pile at a loading area.

facts.text: In the NIOSH haul-truck study, detection of the dump-point berm was deliberately not classified as a nuisance alarm, even when the operator knew the berm was there, because overtravel could send the truck over a high embankment.
facts.quote: Detection of the dump-point berm was deliberately **not** classified as a nuisance even when the operator knew the berm was there, because overtravel could send the truck over a high embankment.

facts.text: In the NIOSH Caterpillar 793B proximity-warning study, an alarm sounded in about 94% of 618 reverse movements.
facts.quote: In 618 reverse movements an alarm sounded about 94% of the time.

facts.text: Of 580 alarms in the NIOSH Caterpillar 793B proximity-warning study, 478 were technically true and 102 (18%) were false.
facts.quote: Of 580 alarms, 478 were technically true and 102 (18%) were false

facts.text: In the NIOSH Caterpillar 793B proximity-warning study, 243 of the 478 technically true alarms were nuisance alarms, representing 42% of all alarms.
facts.quote: 243 of the 478 true alarms (42% of all alarms) were nuisance alarms

facts.text: Only 235 alarms in the NIOSH Caterpillar 793B proximity-warning study warranted immediate action or extra caution: 40% of all alarms, or 41% by Ruff's rounding.
facts.quote: only 235 (40%, or 41% by Ruff's rounding) warranted immediate action or extra caution.

facts.text: The NIOSH Caterpillar 793B proximity-warning study reported no missed detections.
The NIOSH haul-truck alarm results indicate that improving sensor precision alone would not have removed most unwanted alerts; context interpretation was also needed.
facts.quote: Improving sensor precision alone would therefore not have removed most unwanted alerts; context interpretation was also needed.

facts.text: Drivers in the NIOSH haul-truck proximity-warning study found the continuous audible warning annoying because most alarms did not signify danger.
facts.quote: Drivers found the continuous audible warning annoying because most alarms did not signify danger

facts.text: Researchers in the NIOSH haul-truck proximity-warning study found the audible warning function disabled after shifts.
facts.quote: researchers found the audible function disabled after shifts.

facts.text: NIOSH warned that operators may lose confidence in a proximity warning system and start to ignore alarms altogether.
facts.quote: NIOSH warned that operators may "lose confidence in the system and start to ignore alarms altogether" [3, 2].

facts.text: The observation of disabled audible warnings in the NIOSH haul-truck study is partly anecdotal rather than a controlled behavioral endpoint, but provides unusually direct off-road evidence of alarm disengagement.
facts.quote: The disabling observation is partly anecdotal rather than a controlled behavioral endpoint, but it is unusually direct off-road evidence of alarm disengagement.
